summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of Oklahoma City, covering its universities, politics, population growth, sports teams, geography, MAPS redevelopment, broadcasting history and founding. It describes the city as the state capital and largest city, with a 2014 population estimate of 620,602, and it notes its 1889 Land Run settlement and the MAPS downtown revitalization program begun in 1993.
one_line: Overview of Oklahoma City: the state capital's universities, population growth, NBA Thunder, MAPS redevelopment, rivers and lakes, and history from the 1889 Land Run.
key_facts: Oklahoma City is the capital and largest city of the state of Oklahoma and the county seat of Oklahoma County.
The estimated population of Oklahoma City was 620,602 as of July 2014, the largest population the city has ever recorded.
The 2010 census counted 579,999 people in Oklahoma City.
Patience Latting was elected Mayor of Oklahoma City in 1971, becoming the city's first female mayor.
The Oklahoma City Thunder has called Oklahoma City home since the 2008–09 season, when owner Clayton Bennett relocated the franchise from Seattle, Washington.
The Thunder plays home games at the Chesapeake Energy Arena in downtown Oklahoma City.
Oklahoma City was settled on April 22, 1889, when the 'Unassigned Lands' were opened for settlement in an event known as 'The Land Run'.
In 1993, the city passed the Metropolitan Area Projects (MAPS) redevelopment package to rebuild the city's core.
MAPS has exceeded $3 billion in private investment as of 2010.
WKY Radio was the first radio station transmitting west of the Mississippi River and the third radio station in the United States.
WKY-TV (channel 4) went on the air in 1949 and later became the first independently owned television station in the U.S. to broadcast in color.
In May 2015, Oklahoma City recorded 19.48 inches of rainfall, its record-wettest month since record keeping began in 1890.
Oklahoma City was prominently mentioned in Bobby Troup's 1946 jazz classic '(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66'.
The third-largest university in the state, the University of Central Oklahoma, is located in the suburb of Edmond, just north of the city.
Langston University is the state's historically black college (HBCU) and has an urban campus in the eastside section of the city.
